It is distinguished from [Polygon-based CGH generation](13818-polygon-based-cgh-generation.md) and [Layer-Based Holographic Algorithm](13372-layer-based-holographic-algorithm.md) by avoiding large-scale FFT circuits and complex mesh processing, making it highly suitable for hardware implementation [S1, S5].

The claim states that the method (Point-Cloud based CGH) is distinguished from Polygon-based and Layer-Based methods by avoiding large-scale FFT circuits and complex mesh processing, making it suitable for hardware implementation. Source [S5] explicitly supports this: it states that the polygon and layer methods use FFTs and that 'it is difficult to implement large-scale FFT circuits in hardware in parallel,' whereas the point-cloud method is 'suitable for hardware implementation.' It also notes that the split lookup table method (related to complex processing/memory) is unsuitable due to memory requirements, implying the point-cloud method avoids these specific complexities. Source [S1] supports the distinction by noting the point-cloud method has 'relatively simple calculations' compared to layer/polygon methods which have high computational costs for large scenes.

*   Scenes requiring accurate depth cues and natural defocus blur [S6].

The claim states that scenes requiring accurate depth cues and natural defocus blur are associated with Source [S6]. The evidence in Source [S6] explicitly discusses how conventional holograms (nCGH) suffer from 'depth perception distortion' due to weak defocus blur and vivid boundaries (which distort depth cues). It contrasts this with DEH, which displays 'clear defocus blur' and handles depth perception better. The text confirms that the lack of natural defocus blur and the presence of distorted boundaries in nCGH make depth perception difficult, thereby supporting the relevance of these factors (accurate depth cues and natural defocus blur) in the context of the evidence provided.
